rules.statement: Store a client secret as a one-way verifier when its authentication method only compares it (client_secret_basic, client_secret_post); store reversible octets only when the method keys from the secret's UTF-8 octets (client_secret_jwt, HS256 request objects).
rules.why: A comparing method never needs the secret again, so a reversible store only adds a way to leak every secret.
rules.check: Look for client-secret create, rotate, register or seed paths that persist reversible secret material for a comparing method, or a verifier for a keying method.

rules.statement: Don't generate a client_secret through the same path as a symmetric cryptographic key: a key is raw CSPRNG bytes revealed as base64url (JWK `k`), and a client_secret is a random string whose UTF-8 octets are used.
rules.why: UTF8(base64url(raw)) is not the raw bytes, so one generation path for both hands a keying method the wrong key.
rules.check: Look for client_secret issuance that reuses key generation (or the reverse), or that treats the base64url text and the raw bytes as interchangeable.

rules.statement: In client authentication, check a comparing method against stored verifiers only and a keying method against reversible secrets only, and compare with `CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals`.
rules.why: A reversible secret must never authenticate a comparing method, and a comparison that is not constant-time leaks the secret through timing.
rules.check: Look for authentication handlers that compare a presented secret against reversible secrets for basic/post methods, that use verifiers for client_secret_jwt, or that compare with SequenceEqual or ==.

rules.statement: Treat a stored secret verifier whose scheme is unregistered or whose text is malformed as authenticating nothing; never fall back to another comparison.
rules.why: Failing closed keeps a corrupt or unknown verifier from accepting any credential.
rules.check: Look for verifier parsing or scheme lookup that throws unhandled, skips to a plain comparison, or returns success when the scheme is missing or the format is invalid.

rules.statement: Hash a user-supplied secret with a work-factor KDF (for example PBKDF2-SHA256 with at least 600,000 iterations and a 16-byte random salt, octets not normalized), and use a fast hash only for server-generated secrets that have enough entropy.
rules.why: A supplied secret may have low entropy and needs a work factor; a generated one has the entropy for a fast hash.
rules.check: Look for supplied secrets verified with a fast hash, too few iterations, a missing or short salt, or Unicode normalization of the octets.

rules.statement: Validate secret-hashing options (scheme names, iteration counts) at start, and refuse in production an iteration count below the production minimum.
rules.why: A misconfigured work factor should fail at startup rather than weaken every stored verifier silently.
rules.check: Look for KDF or verifier-scheme options without start-time validation, or validation that lets production run below the minimum iteration count.

rules.statement: Run all work-factor secret verifications through one shared concurrency gate with bounded concurrency, queue length and queue timeout, rather than unbounded or one gate per scheme.
rules.why: A work-factor hash costs CPU on every authentication, so verification is a denial-of-service surface; all schemes compete for the same processors.
rules.check: Look for PBKDF2/Argon2 or similar verification calls on a request path that bypass the shared gate, or that add a gate per scheme.

rules.statement: Answer a verification the server refused to run for capacity with `503` `temporarily_unavailable`, `Retry-After`, and `Cache-Control: no-store`, never with `invalid_client`.
rules.why: RFC 6749 section 5.2's invalid_client judges the credential, and a server that could not afford the check made no judgement about it.
rules.check: Look for gate or throttle refusals in client authentication that map to invalid_client or 401, or a 503 without Retry-After and no-store.

rules.statement: When a client has several stored verifiers, check the ones without a work factor before the work-factor ones.
rules.why: This avoids spending expensive hash work when a cheap verifier can settle the match.
rules.check: Look for verifier loops that run KDF-based verifiers before fast-hash ones.

rules.statement: Don't cache the results of secret verification.
rules.why: A cache of accepted secrets is a store of them.
rules.check: Look for memory or distributed caches keyed by presented secrets or holding successful verification outcomes.

rules.statement: Keep a registry of secret-verifier schemes open: a later registration of a name replaces the earlier one, and don't hard-code a closed set of schemes.
rules.why: Another package may need a scheme such as Argon2id or a FIPS-only one.
rules.check: Look for switch statements or enums that close the set of verifier schemes, or a registry that rejects or ignores a re-registration.

rules.statement: Wrap a stored verifier in a secret encoding that is encrypted at rest like every other non-public secret encoding, rather than storing the bare verifier text.
rules.why: Without the envelope a verifier would not get the at-rest encryption every other non-public encoding has.
rules.check: Look for verifier text persisted in plaintext columns, or outside the secret envelope and its protection.

rules.statement: Have secret generation and import share one construction, so an imported or seeded secret is stored in the same shape (encoding, bit length, origin) as a generated one.
rules.why: Separate paths drift and leave seeded secrets in a shape the verifier or the reconciliation logic does not expect.
rules.check: Look for import or seed code that builds stored secrets by hand instead of calling the shared construction, or that omits the origin or key size.

rules.statement: Refuse a client authentication method that keys from the secret without requiring one, and refuse a symmetric request-object signing algorithm for a client whose method only compares its secret.
rules.why: A comparing client stores only a verifier, so it has no octets to key HS256 from.
rules.check: Look for method descriptors or client settings validation that allow UsesClientSecretAsKey without RequiresClientSecret, or HS* request_object_signing_alg values with basic/post authentication.

rules.statement: When a client's authentication method changes, reconcile its stored secrets: convert reversible secrets to verifiers for a comparing method, or, if no unexpired shared secret can serve the new method, issue one in the method's form that replaces the others and reveal it once.
rules.why: Without reconciliation a method switch leaves the client with no usable credential, or leaves reversible secrets it no longer needs.
rules.check: Look for DCR or management update paths that change token_endpoint_auth_method without invoking secret reconciliation.
